Subject: Ephemeral GPU pool guardrails & burst windows for AtlasRetail Dedicated

Hi Sam —

Quick follow-up to our demo yesterday. AtlasRetail's peak traffic during promotional spikes (Blackout Fridays, flash markdowns) is the main driver for the Dedicated sizing question. To move the contract forward we need to agree on practical burst policies and autoscale knobs that keep latency SLOs intact while limiting cost exposure.

I attached two scenarios (baseline vs conservative) — please review but the items I want to align on are:
- Typical burst duration you see (minutes vs hours) and frequency per month
- Peak concurrent generation QPS and average sequence length during bursts
- Whether you need warm KV cache retention across bursts or can tolerate cold starts

Proposed immediate action: a short 30-min call next week with your infra lead + our infra PM (Marissa) to validate the numbers and confirm an amendment clause for ephemeral capacity.

Attachments: proposed-capacity-scenarios.xlsx

Best,
Jordan
Director, Strategic Accounts
Redwood Inference

From: Sam Turner <sam.turner@atlasretail.com>

Date: Mon, 05 Apr 2027 08:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Ephemeral GPU pool guardrails & burst windows for AtlasRetail Dedicated

Jordan —

Thanks for the clear doc. Quick answers:
- Burst duration: typically 15–90 minutes (median ~25m) for product drops, but we get a few multi-hour surges on major campaigns (approx 2–3/month).
- Frequency: ~12–18 bursts/month, but most are short.
- Peak concurrent QPS: around 140 concurrent requests to generation endpoints; average seq length ~450 tokens during promotions.
- KV cache: we rely heavily on short-lived session context — keeping warm cache between bursts reduces latency by ~40%; a cold start is acceptable for non-critical segments but not for the main checkout personalization flow.

Two asks from our procurement/security side:
1) Can we cap monthly ephemeral usage to avoid runaway bills? Prefer a soft cap with automated notifications and hard cap with failover to lower-cost model variant.
2) Need the SLA amendment to spell out burst scaling times and cost multipliers.

Sam
VP Product, AtlasRetail
sam.turner@atlasretail.com

Sam / Jordan —

Thanks for the detail, Sam. From an engineering + cost-control perspective here's a practical guardrail set we recommend for AtlasRetail's Dedicated deployment:

Recommended ephemeral pool and autoscale policy (initial):
- Ephemeral pool baseline: 8 x A100-80GB cards for immediate burst headroom (supports ~160 concurrent gen QPS at your 450-token avg).
- Scale increment: add 4 GPUs per scale-up step; max ephemeral cap: 24 GPUs (to protect against runaway).
- Cooldown: 60s steady-state before scale-down; require 2 consecutive cooldown windows to remove a step (helps with oscillation during noisy bursts).
- Burst window ceiling: allow up to 30 peak minutes per burst without cost penalties; multi-hour events count as separate bursts and trigger notifications and approval flows.
- Monthly soft cap: 280 ephemeral GPU-minutes per month (alerts at 70% / 90%); hard cap at 600 GPU-minutes that triggers automatic fallback to the low-cost model variant (int8/int4 profile) for non-critical routes.

Operational notes:
- To preserve KV cache for the checkout personalization flow, we recommend pinning a small warm pool (2 GPUs) that stay resident (billed as reserved but sized small). Ephemeral pool scales additional GPUs that do not retain KV state.
- Fallback model variants: we can configure per-route fallback to a quantized variant with explicit quality gates — useful for cost containment during hard caps.
- Instrumentation: we'll emit token-level cost and per-route latency traces to your monitoring stack; HubSpot deal will include a dashboard link for live burn rates.

Attachments in this thread: SLA amendment draft (we'll drop the burst definitions into section 3.2).

If this looks good, Jordan and I will prep the exact amendment language and a short change-order SOW showing the ephemeral pricing delta.

-Marissa
Product Manager, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference
